papers.title: Execution-Boundary Governance
papers.subtitle: A Runtime Control Model for Autonomous Systems
papers.abstract: Current AI governance frameworks focus on policy, oversight, documentation, transparency, and post-execution accountability. As autonomous systems gain the ability to execute transactions, invoke tools, modify records, move funds, and trigger physical actions, governance must operate within finite latency budgets. This paper proposes Execution-Boundary Governance (EBG), a framework that distinguishes interpretive governance from executable governance and introduces the Executable Governance Kernel (EGK) — a minimal, deterministic, tamper-resistant mechanism operating at the final control point

papers.title: Upstream
papers.subtitle: Where Human-in-the-Loop Goes at Machine Speed
papers.abstract: Software now takes consequential action on its own. It places orders, moves money, approves claims, and grants access, and it does all of it faster than anyone can review. Governance that cannot be present at the moment of action has to be settled beforehand, and written so a machine can apply it without asking. This paper examines what happens when organisations try to do that at scale. The usual conclusion is that the human leaves the loop. That conclusion is wrong. papers.title: The Execution Surface
papers.subtitle: Why Distributed Compute Cannot Be Shared
papers.abstract: Compute is moving outward. That argument is over, and this paper does not make it. It starts from the condition itself and asks what kind of thing is being built. The answer is a planetary execution surface: a continuous layer of local compute running from gigawatt campuses down to milliwatt endpoints, thickest wherever consequences occur.
